newsitem.title: LESOTHO: Lesotho's army quells police mutiny.
newsitem.headline: Lesotho's army quells police mutiny.

text.p: Lesotho army troops ended an 11-day-old police mutiny on Sunday, overwhelming the rebels with a dawn onslaught of heavy gunfire after which at least 30 officers surrendered to troops.
"Now everything is okay. It is over. They (the renegade police officers) have all been taken," an army major on the scene told Reuters. He said nobody was hurt.

Heavy gunfire erupted in the southern African kingdom's capital early on Sunday as army troops moved in to end the mutiny. Western diplomats had earlier said the crisis could lead to a coup against Prime Minister Ntsu Mokhehle's government.
Two armoured cars speeded around the police headquarters firing at the building with mounted machineguns amidst bursts of shouts over a loudhailer to the rebels: "Come out, come out."
"We have 33 people who have given themselves up including (Second Lieutenant) Modise, who is the leader of the rebels," a Western diplomat said.
The major, who refused to give his name, said the rebel police officers were being held at an army base some two km (one mile) outside the capital Maseru.
"Nobody was killed and nobody was wounded. We have arrested about 30 people. They were taken to the Lesotho Defence Force camp," the major said. He would not give details of the operation.

A Reuters correspondent said police used heavy-calibre machineguns, automatic rifles and hand grenades in the attack. The policemen fired back, apparently using mainly semi-automatic rifles. Intermittent gunfire echoed around the capital some three hours after shooting started with a heavy 15-minute barrage at 6.30 a.m. (0430 GMT).

The road in front of the charge office was littered with spent cartridges. The walls were pockmarked with bullet holes and the windows were shattered. Inside the charge office there were also cartridge casings and empty ammunition cases.
Curious spectators were walking into single-storey offices and milled outside as the soldiers were preparing to move out.
The headquarters building, a tall office block some 100 metres (yards) further, had shattered window panes but seemed to have sustained little damage.
The mutiny began when eight officers seized control of the police headquarters in Lesotho, which is surrounded by and reliant on the region's economic giant South Africa.
Up to 60 other policemen were reported to have joined them in occupying the police headquarters since their siege began, but this figure appears to have been exaggerated.
South Africa on Saturday threw its weight behind the Lesotho government and said it should quell the mutiny which had led to a police strike by late Thursday.

The army major said they had first tried to negotiate with the rebel policemen. "We tried to convince them to come out and that we wouldn't fight them. We started shooting about an hour later to get them out of the offices. We were not trying to kill them but just trying to frighten them," he said.
The Lesotho government has not yet commented publicly on Sunday's offensive.
